Tamburlaine. Christopher Marlowe's epic chronicle written in two parts between 1587 and 1588, depicting a Scythian shepherd who rises through military genius and will-to-power to conquer much of the known world. The play launches Marlowe's characteristic blank verse, the mighty line, and celebrates an amoral conqueror who brooks no rival, embodying Renaissance admiration for power and the charismatic individual unconstrained by morality or divine sanction.

Tamburlaine, a nomadic shepherd, conquers armies across Asia, Persia, Egypt, and the Ottoman Empire through tactical brilliance, personal magnetism, and ruthless ambition. Marlowe's blank verse elevates Tamburlaine's rhetoric to near-lyrical heights, his speeches asserting the self-made man and the conquest of fate through will. The play celebrates power itself, as Tamburlaine defeats not one rival but successive kingdoms.

He speaks of Zenocrate, a Damascus princess, with sensual reverence, yet subordinates love to conquest. He defeats Bajazeth, the Ottoman emperor, and humiliates him into slavery, forcing the divine-right monarch to serve as his footstool—a theatrical emblem of might overturning hierarchy.

Part Two introduces the limits of will. Tamburlaine ages, grows ill, and confronts death. His son Calyphas proves a coward, triggering Tamburlaine's rage and the first signs of his own mortality. The play features spectacular staging—walls burning, kings on golden thrones pulled by conquered monarchs—rendering Tamburlaine's dominion in visual grandeur.

Yet Tamburlaine never repents. He dies in harness, still commanding armies, embodying the protagonist for whom conquest is both means and end. His triumph over Alexander the Great's own historical parallel establishes the archetype: the self-made ruler, unchecked by law or morality. Marlowe's first major success and most grandiose work revolutionized dramatic verse and left an indelible mark on how Renaissance drama conceives of power and ambition.
